newsitem.title: HONG KONG: British Gurkha Chief says PLA eager for HK success.
newsitem.headline: British Gurkha Chief says PLA eager for HK success.

text.p: The British commander of Nepalese Gurkhas helping to hand Hong Kong to China says People's Liberation Army troops are eager to succeed in a sensitive new role here, after the Tiananmen Square massacre.

"The PLA will be just fine," said Lieutenant-Colonel Jeremy Ellis, commander of the Queen's Gurkha Signals Regiment which pulls out after the June 30 handover ends 156 years of colonial rule in Hong Kong.

"They are very keen to get it right and have listened to what we say. The key is they want to do well," he told Reuters on Wednesday night at an emotion-charged concert by British massed bands paying a nostalgic farewell to Hong Kong.
The prospective sight of green-uniformed PLA troops on the streets of Hong Kong is a highly charged political issue.

It revives memories among many Hong Kong people of Beijing's 1989 Tiananmen killings when PLA troops turned their guns on unarmed students fighting for democracy. One million people took to the streets of the colony to protest afterwards.
Britain fought a protracted diplomatic battle with Beijing before eventually agreeing that 500 extra armed troops should be allowed into Hong Kong just before the handover.
The first batch of 200 unarmed PLA troops arrived by bus in Hong Kong more than a month ago in a low-key operation.

Ellis, acknowledging that PLA troops were treading in a political minefield in their new role, said: "In China presumably they are quite isolated. Here they won't be. They are quite as disciplined as us."
The Gurkha commander has faced an emotional rollercoaster with the gradual whittling down in Hong Kong of the frontline mercenaries recruited from the Himalayan kingdom of Nepal.

The Gurkhas, who have fought for Britain in every major conflict of the 20th century, have served under British colours in Hong Kong for nearly half a century. At one time, more than 3,000 were stationed in the colony.
The Gurkhas, who have now served the British crown for 180 years, face an uncertain future as Britain reins in defence commitments in the new post-Cold War era.
"In the last two years we have gone from 600 to 33 on the final day here. It is not something one volunteers to go through," Ellis said.
After four tours of duty in Hong Kong where he also met his wife, Ellis said: "I am very sad to go but we will do it properly. The people of Britain will be proud of us."
"Hong Kong has a magnetic attraction you cannot resist," he said. "I hope the Chinese look at us with affection. This is a golden goose for everyone and I hope it stays so."
